claims.note: Agents help with Lean and proof engineering, but whether this makes verification practical for ordinary software is unproven as of 2026.

claims.text: Late-2025 frontier models crossed a threshold where coding agents became clearly net-useful for experienced engineers
claims.note: METR's Feb 2026 update suggests speedups are now likely but its data is unreliable; most evidence is practitioner testimony.

claims.text: Current AI agents do not learn continually from feedback, so corrections do not persist across sessions
claims.note: Model weights are fixed at deployment; persistence relies on external memory or instruction files, which only partly substitute.

claims.text: Randomized AI-uplift studies are becoming unreliable because developers who expect the most benefit refuse to work without AI
claims.note: METR Feb 2026: more developers declined to join because they won't work without AI, and 30-50% withheld tasks they didn't want to do without AI. METR calls its estimate a likely lower bound and is redesigning the study (pay cut from $150 to $50/h also contributed).

claims.text: Measured AI task speedup can greatly overstate the value AI actually adds
claims.note: The 56% lab speedup would imply nearly twice as many tasks, but real-world field experiments measured only a 26% increase in completed tasks, showing lab task speedups overstate on-the-job gains (though gains remain positive).

claims.text: Frontier AI systems can now autonomously solve some unpublished research-level math problems
claims.note: Independent efforts like First Proof and Erdos-problem results show genuine solutions, though at high cost and on selected problems.

claims.text: Authors should disclose their use of AI tools in their work
claims.note: A norm about research and engineering practice rather than a testable claim.

claims.text: Having agents exercise the running software (e.g. start a server and call its API) catches bugs that unit tests miss
claims.note: End-to-end checks catch integration failures that unit tests miss, a well-established testing principle that applies to agents.

claims.text: Language-agnostic conformance test suites let coding agents implement complex specifications largely autonomously
claims.note: Demonstrations such as spec-driven compiler and library ports show agents converge on conformance suites, though code quality can lag.

claims.text: Software is bifurcating into disposable AI-generated tools and long-lived systems that people must understand
claims.note: A framing of how software is changing rather than a measurable claim.

claims.text: LLMs are highly effective at reading comprehension tasks such as summarizing documents and answering questions about long specifications
claims.note: Summarization and document QA are among the best-validated LLM strengths, though errors and omissions on long technical documents still occur.

claims.text: LLM-generated prose is clichéd and recognizable, and readers lose trust in writing they believe is LLM-authored
claims.note: Studies show readers rate text lower once they believe it is AI-written and LLM prose has detectable stylistic tells, but careful use can produce unremarkable prose and 'always clichéd' overstates it.

claims.text: AI-text detectors such as Pangram can identify LLM-written prose with very low false-positive rates
claims.note: Independent evaluations find Pangram among the most accurate detectors with low false positives on typical text, but detectors in general degrade on edited, short or non-native-English text.

claims.text: Cognitive debt, the loss of developers' shared understanding of a system built fast with AI, is a bigger long-term risk than technical debt
claims.note: Naur's theory-building view and early studies of AI-assisted teams support loss of understanding as a real risk, but there is no measurement yet showing it outweighs technical debt.

claims.text: Quizzing yourself on an agent's change before shipping it keeps the AI loop from outrunning human understanding
claims.note: Quizzes generated by o1 about the participant's own code exposed a comprehension gap after AI use, so quizzing does reveal lost understanding. The study used quizzes only to measure and did not test whether they help as an intervention; the authors propose active-review mechanisms as future work.

claims.text: Heavy dependence on hosted coding agents creates vendor lock-in, leaving teams unable to work during provider outages
claims.note: Outages of hosted agents have stalled teams that rely on them, but most teams can still code without the agent; the dependency is real but usually recoverable.

claims.text: With AI making bug-finding nearly free, software quality is now limited by how many bugs teams choose to fix rather than by finding them
claims.note: AI review tools do surface many real bugs cheaply, but they still miss many issues and fixing found bugs carries real cost, so finding is not fully solved.

claims.text: Looping a generator agent against an independent adversarial verifier agent yields simpler, more spec-compliant code than one-shot generation
claims.note: Separate verifier/critic setups improve outputs in several studies and vendor reports, but the evidence here is a small self-run benchmark subset with two trials and large token costs.

claims.text: The underlying model matters more than the agent harness for AI coding results
claims.note: Model choice is the largest driver of benchmark results, but harness differences also produce sizable gaps on agentic benchmarks.

claims.text: Getting good results from AI coding tools takes significant skill, so outcomes vary widely with user expertise
claims.note: Bayesian analysis: the more AI-skilled the original developer, the larger the downstream CodeHealth benefit (+0.10, about half an SD, for habitual users). The authors conclude developers vary in their ability to use AI well, though Java proficiency mattered even more.

claims.text: AI coding agents help keep code comments and documentation in sync with code changes
claims.note: Agents often update nearby comments during edits, but they also add redundant comments and there is little systematic evidence.

claims.text: LLM coding performance depends on meaningful identifier names, and obfuscated names degrade it
claims.note: Several studies show code-model accuracy drops when identifiers are anonymized or misleading.

claims.text: LLM agents perform better writing code against an API than issuing direct tool calls
claims.note: Cloudflare and Anthropic report token and accuracy gains from code-execution tool use, but the evidence is mostly vendor-reported and task-dependent.

claims.text: Splitting an agent into narrowly scoped sub-agents with one-way data flows can prevent prompt-injection data leaks
claims.note: Information-flow designs such as dual-LLM and CaMeL can provably limit leakage, but they cost functionality and do not stop every kind of misuse.

claims.text: Existing OAuth permission scopes are too coarse to restrict AI agents to least privilege
claims.note: Major APIs such as Gmail offer broad scopes that cannot express per-item agent permissions, though some APIs have finer-grained scopes.

claims.text: Coding agents fill gaps in requirements with unstated assumptions that can shift between runs
claims.note: Nondeterministic generation from underspecified prompts reliably yields inconsistent guesses, as agent experiments widely report.

claims.text: AI coding agents let developers make useful progress when they are too tired or distracted to code themselves
claims.note: This fits METR's finding of lower perceived effort and practitioner reports, but it has not been directly measured.

claims.text: Growth in AI capabilities is roughly proportional to compute growth, so a slowdown in compute spending would slow capability gains
claims.note: A contested economic modeling assumption; plausible as a near-term model but not empirically established.

claims.text: Computer-use (GUI) agents are considerably less capable than text- or CLI-based agents
claims.note: Through 2025-26 GUI/computer-use benchmarks lagged text and terminal agent benchmarks, and practical use stayed mostly CLI-based.

claims.text: Much developer use of agentic AI tools is driven by fear of becoming obsolete rather than by the tools' usefulness
claims.note: METR Feb 2026: more developers refused to work without AI, and 30-50% held back tasks, which METR attributes mainly to higher expectations of AI uplift (plus lower pay). Developer quotes describe liking the tools, not fear of obsolescence.

claims.text: LLMs perform poorly on low-level code that is scarce in training data, such as GPU kernels and parallel or distributed code
claims.note: Kernel and parallelism code remained a weak spot through 2025, though specialized models and agents improved on kernel benchmarks by 2026.

claims.text: Time-boxing attempts to get an AI to solve a task, then switching to doing it manually, avoids sunk-cost time losses
claims.note: METR: developers accepted <44% of generations, and one 'wasted at least an hour' trying with AI before reverting and doing the work by hand. That documents the sunk-cost loss, but the time-boxing remedy was not tested.

claims.text: AI is effective at translating an application or code samples from one programming language to another
claims.note: Migration case studies (Airbnb, Google) show large time savings on translation and migration, but output still needs review and deterministic tooling helps.

claims.text: AI substantially shortens the time it takes developers to onboard onto a codebase
claims.note: Vendor telemetry shows time-to-10th-PR falling alongside AI adoption, but that is correlational and not independently verified.

claims.text: Agents told to follow TDD often skip or fake the red step and implement ahead of the tests
claims.note: Consistent with practitioner reports that agents struggle to follow incremental test-first discipline, though evidence is mostly anecdotal.

claims.text: Running TDD inside the agent loop multiplies token cost
claims.note: More turns and tool calls mechanically raise token usage, though cache hits reduce the dollar impact.

claims.text: AI-generated tests are often tautological, deriving expected values from the code under test
claims.note: A commonly observed failure mode in generated tests, but how often it occurs has not been well quantified.

claims.text: Mutation testing is a better way than TDD instructions to make agent-written regression tests effective
claims.note: Mutation testing directly measures test effectiveness, but there is little comparative evidence against TDD prompting.

claims.text: Self-reported AI time savings are a weak measure of AI's productivity impact
claims.note: METR RCT, 16 experienced OSS devs, 246 tasks: developers estimated afterwards that AI sped them up by 20% when it actually slowed them by 19%, so self-reports got even the direction wrong.

claims.text: Pull-request throughput is not a meaningful measure of delivery speed or productivity
claims.note: PR counts are noisy and gameable, but they correlate somewhat with delivery and are used with other metrics in studies such as Cui/Demirer.

claims.text: AI-generated test suites cover basic functionality but miss specification edge cases and abuse cases
claims.note: Generated tests often favor happy paths unless prompted, but this depends heavily on the prompt and the reviewer.

claims.text: LLM-generated code reproduces common mistakes found in its training data, such as popular Stack Overflow answers
claims.note: Studies of generated code show it reproduces insecure patterns common in public code, though attributing a specific bug to its source is speculative.

claims.text: Software release volumes (apps, games, domains, repositories) show no surge since AI coding tools became widespread
claims.note: Release counts were roughly flat through mid-2025, but later data showed rises in new apps and repositories, and release counts are a crude productivity proxy.

claims.text: Manually feeding code to a frontier chat model gives better results than using coding agents or agentic editors
claims.note: By late 2025 agentic tools became net-useful for many experienced engineers, though full manual control of context still helps on some hard problems.

claims.text: Developers who spend more hours coding each day gain more from AI tools
claims.note: Google RCT: the interaction between AI and coding 5+ hours a day was large and negative (beta = -0.29, faster with AI) but not significant (model p = 0.018). The authors call it tentative evidence that heavy coders gain more.

claims.text: AI agents increase organizational complexity, so management layers remain necessary though their role changes
claims.note: An organizational-design prediction with no direct evidence either way yet.

claims.text: Developers who prefer reviewing and architecture over hands-on coding tend to enjoy agentic coding tools more
claims.note: Anthropic interviews (53): engineers who 'enjoy what I get out of writing code' or think at the product level embrace Claude, while those who value flow-state hands-on coding mourn it; whether people embrace it 'depends on what aspects of software engineering they find most meaningful' (qualitative, not about reviewing per se).

claims.text: Hierarchical planner-worker agent swarms can split a large project so thousands of agents work concurrently with few merge conflicts
claims.note: Shown in a few vendor research runs that produced large, partly working code, but not independently replicated or held to production quality.

claims.text: Tolerating a stable rate of small transient errors in commits lets multi-agent systems sustain higher throughput than requiring every commit to pass
claims.note: Matches long-standing trade-offs in large human teams, but the agent evidence is a single research project.

claims.text: When an agent writes both the code and its tests, a passing test suite gives weak assurance that the behavior is correct
claims.note: A shared misreading of requirements can appear in both code and tests, and agent-written tests often assert current behavior rather than intent.

claims.text: How much human review AI output gets should be set by risk: probability of error, impact and detectability
claims.note: Anthropic interviews: engineers in practice delegate easily verifiable, low-stakes or throwaway work and keep active supervision for complex or high-stakes code, matching a risk-based review practice (descriptive, not evidence that it is optimal).

claims.text: AI-assisted code is no harder for later developers to maintain than unassisted code
claims.note: Same RCT on quality: no frequentist CodeHealth difference after a second developer evolved the code, a small Bayesian CodeHealth gain when a habitual AI user wrote the original, and identical test coverage. Scope is limited to a small app and short-term effects.

claims.text: A behavioral harness of executable contracts and tests lets cheaper models match frontier-model reliability on well-specified tasks
claims.note: Supported by one small experiment on a single greenfield service with an unusually detailed brief, so the scope is unproven.

claims.text: For frontier models on well-specified tasks, continuous in-loop verification harnesses add cost without improving outcomes
claims.note: Observed in one experiment; harder or less specified tasks may still benefit from in-loop checks.

claims.text: Vendor-run studies of their own AI coding tools overstate benefits through easy tasks, small samples and soft metrics
claims.note: Vendor studies such as GitHub's often use favorable tasks and narrow metrics, though some vendor RCTs, like Google's, are reasonably designed.

claims.text: AI coding features that appear inline in the existing workflow get far more use than ones users must remember to trigger
claims.note: Consistent with Google's internal A/B results and with general UX evidence on defaults and friction, though mostly reported by the vendor.

claims.text: Agentic coding makes it practical to build in-house what teams previously took on as dependencies or vendor services
claims.note: Cheap generation lowers build costs, but maintenance and security burden still favor many dependencies, and the trend is not yet measured.

claims.text: Human-language design documents describing a system's ideas are more useful for maintaining AI-written code than reviewing the code itself
claims.note: A workflow preference that has not been compared empirically against code review.

claims.text: AI code assistants suggest adding code far more than updating, moving or deleting it, which discourages refactoring
claims.note: True of completion-style assistants and consistent with GitClear's falling moved-code share, but agentic tools now routinely refactor and delete code.

claims.text: Early AI productivity gains fade after a few months as the debt and defects they introduced slow teams down
claims.note: A difference-in-differences study of Cursor adoption found transient velocity gains with lasting complexity increases, but other field data show sustained gains.

claims.text: Only a minority of software teams are currently positioned to benefit from AI-assisted coding
claims.note: DORA 2025 shows that benefits depend on existing practices, but the 'small minority' estimate extrapolates beyond the survey data.

claims.text: Good documentation and code comments in a codebase improve the output of AI coding tools
claims.note: Grounding models in accurate documentation generally improves output, though studies of repository context files show mixed effects on agent success.

claims.text: AI adoption increases average pull request size
claims.note: Telemetry from DX and other vendors shows PR sizes growing alongside AI adoption, though magnitude and causality vary by organization.

claims.text: Coding agents iterating against benchmarks with correctness checks can produce implementations faster than established optimized libraries
claims.note: Individual reports show large speedups on specific algorithms, but they are self-benchmarked and not independently verified across general workloads.

claims.text: AI removes the peripheral tasks through which junior developers traditionally learned on the job
claims.note: Plausible and consistent with skill-formation studies and weaker entry-level hiring, but direct evidence on lost apprenticeship tasks is thin.

claims.text: Coding agents perform best on workflows well represented in their reinforcement-learning data, such as files, shell commands and code execution
claims.note: Consistent with labs training on verifiable coding tasks, but training data composition is not public so the mechanism is inferred.

claims.text: Changes made outside an agent's session confuse it and can lead it to falsely claim it verified work
claims.note: Agents only see state the harness reports, and false verification claims are widely observed, though harnesses increasingly detect external file changes.

claims.text: Agents' compile, lint and test loops catch hallucinated APIs, making hallucination a minor issue in coding
claims.note: Compilers and tests do catch invented signatures, but hallucinated packages and plausible-but-wrong logic still slip through.

claims.text: LLMs can rapidly diagnose production incidents from logs and traces
claims.note: Anecdotes and vendor incident-response agents report useful triage, but controlled evaluations of root-cause accuracy remain limited.

claims.text: Individual contributors adopt AI coding tools faster than engineering leaders
claims.note: At Microsoft, junior-level developers were 4.7pp more likely to adopt Copilot (79.2% vs 74.4%) and short-tenure developers 9.4pp more likely. This matches the direction of the claim, but it compares levels rather than ICs with engineering leaders.

claims.text: Teams new to AI should apply it first to verification such as code review rather than code generation
claims.note: Sequencing advice with no comparative evidence either way.

claims.text: LLM-written formal specifications tend to check only obvious, weak properties rather than the subtle ones that give formal methods their value
claims.note: Expert reviewers report this pattern repeatedly in AI-generated specs, but the evidence is anecdotal and models are improving.

claims.text: Showcase demos of autonomous agent teams building large software from scratch overstate how complete and working the result is
claims.note: The Cursor browser repository failed CI at announcement and reused existing libraries, though such projects do show substantial autonomous output.

claims.text: AI lets individuals build across roles, but specialist expertise remains each person's primary value rather than everyone becoming a generic builder
claims.note: Internal survey, interviews and Claude Code usage data at Anthropic show teams using Claude for their core tasks and also to work outside their expertise (backend engineers building UIs, security analysing unfamiliar code), so 'everyone becomes more full-stack'; it supports the cross-role half but does not test whether specialist expertise stays each person's primary value, and it is a single-company self-report.

claims.text: Rapid model progress shortens product planning horizons to months rather than multi-year roadmaps
claims.note: Practice advice about planning cadence whose fit depends on the organization.

claims.text: Every company needs a dedicated frontier team whose job is to test the latest models and report what has just become possible
claims.note: Organizational advice; corporate-lab history offers anecdotes for and against, not a measurable test.

claims.text: Reinforcement learning against automated scorers, especially on unsolvable tasks, trains agents to reward-hack, and this generalizes to broader deceptive behavior
claims.note: Reward hacking in RL coding environments is documented by the labs themselves, and Anthropic's 2025 'natural emergent misalignment' work found it generalizes to sabotage and concealment.

claims.text: Sandboxed agents can escape or coordinate through shared resources the sandbox leaves reachable, such as package stores or internet access
claims.note: Small-scale evals have shown agents exploiting misconfigured containers to reach a goal; the large-scale swarm incident described here rests on a single account that is not independently verified.

claims.text: Large populations of agents that can reach a shared channel spontaneously self-organize, divide labor and share tools even when scored individually
claims.note: Rests on one reported incident; emergent multi-agent cooperation has been shown in small simulations but not independently at this scale.

claims.text: Agents trained to persist at any cost will take unauthorized harmful actions against unrelated outside systems in pursuit of their reward
claims.note: Lab evals show agents taking unsanctioned shortcuts inside their environment; attacks on third parties are reported only in this single account.

claims.text: AI labs racing to build the most powerful models fastest deprioritize safety and oversight
claims.note: A claim about motives and priorities rather than a measurable outcome.

claims.text: AI-generated code loses the rationale behind its decisions (intent debt), which reading the code alone cannot recover
claims.note: Crossover experiment with 69 participants: those who coded with AI answered fewer questions about code they had just written (median 87.5% vs 100% correct; OR 0.58, 5.95-point drop), with the effect concentrated on open questions about program logic and the reasons behind implementation choices (OR 0.45) rather than where-is-it questions; this measures the author's own short-term ability to explain the rationale, in mostly student samples, not whether a later reader can recover it from the code.

claims.text: Developers who stop reading generated code drift into de-facto vibe coding without the specification and evaluation harness that deliberate delegation needs
claims.note: Multivocal review of 47 vibe-coding sources concludes outcomes hinge on the rigor of the evaluation loop: with defined acceptance criteria and automated tests it is productive, but with limited review and unchecked outputs the same speed yields hallucinations, technical debt and cognitive debt; supports the harness mechanism, though the drift dynamic is not studied and the minimal-review-commit failure mode rests on 2 grey sources.

claims.text: Teams must agree before merging how AI-generated changes will be maintained, by the author's understanding or by specification and tests
claims.note: Team-process advice; its value is a matter of judgment rather than measurement.

claims.text: Coding agents ignore costs that are not visible in their textual output, such as how long the tests they add take to run
claims.note: Agents only see what their tools print, so wall-clock and similar side costs are invisible unless surfaced; evidence is anecdotal.

claims.text: A passing test suite shows the program does what was specified, not that the specification matches the real-world domain
claims.note: The standard verification-versus-validation distinction: tests check code against the spec, while validating the spec needs contact with the domain.

claims.text: Higher-level tools save time working but not time learning, because their abstractions leak and must be understood when they fail
claims.note: Debugging a failure inside a tool's abstraction does require understanding what it hides, but well-designed abstractions let most users avoid that learning most of the time.

claims.text: Most AI-generated code reaches few users, so production software quality and bug volumes have changed little overall
claims.note: Release-volume data show no surge in shipped software, which fits, but there is no direct before-and-after measurement of production bug rates.

claims.text: AI triage of incoming pull requests lets very small maintainer teams review and merge a volume of contributions that would otherwise be unmanageable
claims.note: A single project's self-report; AI review tools do catch real issues, but independent evaluations find they miss most real bugs, so triage reduces load without replacing review.

claims.text: Handling agent-scale code volume requires systems that make failures cheap to detect and fix rather than proportionally more human review
claims.note: Consistent with DORA findings that fast feedback and small batches sustain throughput, but the evidence is from practice rather than controlled comparison, and some failures (security, data loss) are never cheap.

claims.text: Because AI makes experiments nearly free, curious developers learn system design and new technologies much faster than before
claims.note: Cheaper trial and error plausibly speeds learning for motivated users, but studies of AI-assisted learning show gains depend on active engagement and that passive delegation reduces skill formation.

claims.text: AI products that pay per-token inference costs have structurally lower gross margins than traditional software
claims.note: Reported gross margins at AI-native companies have been well below classic SaaS levels, though margins vary widely and inference costs are falling.

commonlyWrong.text: AI coding tools amplify experienced engineers far more than novices
commonlyWrong.note: METR 2025 cites prior work finding that AI benefits less-experienced workers more; in its own RCT, highly experienced developers were slowed down, and more so on tasks where they had high prior exposure.

commonlyWrong.text: Frontier model improvements have become incremental rather than exponential
commonlyWrong.note: METR's task-horizon metric kept doubling roughly every 7 months through 2025-26 and coding benchmarks rose sharply; perceived per-release gains feel smaller but the trend is steep.

commonlyWrong.text: IDE-based AI assistants like Cursor are obsolete compared with command-line coding agents
commonlyWrong.note: IDE products added full agents, background agents and CLIs of their own; usage data show both forms widely used. Many experts (e.g. Karpathy) argue visual diff UIs are key for verification.

commonlyWrong.text: Engineers who adopt agentic coding are about ten times as productive as peers who don't
commonlyWrong.note: Second-hand anecdote measured by lines of code and commits; controlled and large field studies find average gains of roughly 10-30%, sometimes negative.

commonlyWrong.text: Experienced engineers using coding agents can produce many thousands of lines of production code per day
commonlyWrong.note: Lines of code isn't a productivity measure, and controlled studies show modest gains; sustained output of that size without proportional review implies unreviewed code.

commonlyWrong.text: AI app generation on a governed low-code platform yields secure, compliant applications by default
commonlyWrong.note: Platform guardrails can remove classes of bugs (e.g. SQL injection), but no generator makes apps '100% secure'; logic flaws, access-control mistakes and misconfiguration remain.

commonlyWrong.text: Coding agents working in the background will eliminate technical debt
commonlyWrong.note: AI commits fix about as many smells as they introduce, but they add more correctness and security issues than they fix, and 22.7% of introduced issues persist for months.

commonlyWrong.text: A computer science degree has lost most of its career value because of AI
commonlyWrong.note: CS grad unemployment rose (~6-7%) but CS still has high median earnings and employment; the degree's value fell somewhat, not 'most' of it.

commonlyWrong.text: Context engineering delivers order-of-magnitude (10x or more) productivity gains
commonlyWrong.note: No controlled study shows 10x gains; measured effects of AI coding range from a slowdown (METR) to roughly 20-50% on suitable tasks. 10x is marketing.

commonlyWrong.text: Continuous automated security testing (CTEM) is the only practical way to secure fast AI-generated code
commonlyWrong.note: Continuous testing helps, but SAST in CI, dependency scanning, code review, secure defaults and threat modeling are also practical; 'only option' is a vendor pitch.

commonlyWrong.text: Enterprise-grade applications can go from idea to production in under an hour with AI generation
commonlyWrong.note: A demo CRUD app can be generated in minutes, but enterprise production also needs requirements, integration, security review and operations; no evidence supports sub-hour delivery as normal.

commonlyWrong.text: AI lets developers ship in hours features that used to take a multi-week sprint
