contested.text: Specs-to-code workflows that ignore the generated code do not work; developers must keep understanding and shaping the code
contested.note: Ignoring code entirely leads to drift and debt in real codebases; but spec-driven approaches with code review do work.

contested.text: Test-driven development (red-green-refactor) makes AI agents produce better code and tests
contested.note: Tests-first gives agents a target and limits test-cheating; evidence is mostly anecdotal and it does not suit all code (e.g. UI).

contested.text: Goal or loop commands that re-prompt an agent until a goal is met let it work through a backlog unattended
contested.note: Goal/loop features keep agents going through backlogs, but unattended runs drift or game checks without good verification; works when acceptance tests are strong.

contested.text: In AI-assisted development the specification, not the code, should be the authoritative source of truth
contested.note: Specs help align agents, but code is still what runs; specs drift from implementation unless continuously maintained, and practitioners like Pocock report specs-only workflows failing.

contested.text: Frontier model improvements have become incremental rather than exponential
contested.note: METR's task-horizon metric kept doubling roughly every 7 months through 2025-26 and coding benchmarks rose sharply; perceived per-release gains feel smaller but the trend is steep.

contested.text: Open-weight coding models now handle typical coding tasks reasonably well, though they trail the best closed models
contested.note: Qwen3-Coder, Kimi K2 and GLM 4.5/4.6 posted strong SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench results in 2025 while generally trailing frontier closed models.

contested.text: The post-2022 drop in developer hiring was driven mainly by interest rates and pandemic over-hiring rather than AI
contested.note: The 2022-23 decline began before ChatGPT and tracks rate hikes and over-hiring; most economists attribute it mainly to macro factors, though AI may weigh on junior roles since 2024.

contested.text: Measuring engineers by AI token usage (leaderboards, spend targets) drives wasteful 'token maxing'
contested.note: Goodhart's law applies: Orosz reports leaderboards and spend targets at large firms prompting busywork; consistent with past experience of line-of-code metrics.

contested.text: A simple, self-owned AI coding workflow works better than adopting a heavyweight off-the-shelf agent framework
contested.note: Owning and understanding your workflow helps you debug it, and many practitioners report framework bloat; but there is no comparative evidence, and frameworks can be a good starting point.

contested.text: AI coding assistants improve developer satisfaction and help them stay in flow
contested.note: Self-reported surveys consistently show higher satisfaction and flow, but these are vendor-run perception data and other reports show added review burden and fatigue.

contested.text: AI-generated code drifts from a codebase's established conventions
contested.note: Without enough context, models fall back to common internet patterns; instruction files and indexing reduce but do not remove this.

contested.text: GitHub Copilot makes developers complete tasks about 55% faster
contested.note: Origin of the figure: 95 Upwork freelancers writing a JavaScript HTTP server finished 55.8% faster with Copilot (95% CI 21-89%), true for this one standardized greenfield task but not shown for real work.

contested.text: IDE-based AI assistants like Cursor are obsolete compared with command-line coding agents
contested.note: IDE products added full agents, background agents and CLIs of their own; usage data show both forms widely used. Many experts (e.g. Karpathy) argue visual diff UIs are key for verification.

contested.text: The measured AI slowdown is mainly an artifact of older models and would disappear with newer ones
contested.note: METR Feb 2026: METR believes developers are likely more sped up in early 2026. Returning developers show an 18% time reduction (CI -38% to +9%) and new recruits a 4% reduction (CI -15% to +9%), but selection effects make this 'very weak evidence', and models are not separated from other changes.

contested.text: Natural-language prompts have become a new programming paradigm ('Software 3.0')
contested.note: Many sources frame vibe coding as a new paradigm with natural language as the primary interface (67% of 36 RQ1 sources use an NL-to-code framing); this reflects how it is framed, not a demonstrated paradigm shift.

contested.text: Predictions that AI would write around 90% of all code within months did not come true on schedule
contested.note: Industry-wide, AI did not write ~90% of code by late 2025; but some AI-heavy teams (including at Anthropic) reported 70-90%+, so it partly came true in narrow settings.

contested.text: Running many coding agents in parallel is not yet productive for most developers
contested.note: Review and merge overhead limits parallel agents for most people today, but structured setups (worktrees, independent tasks) are productive for some.

contested.text: Summarizing or pruning conversation history keeps long agent sessions effective and cheaper
contested.note: Summarization cuts cost and keeps sessions going, but lossy summaries can drop details that matter; quality depends on what is kept.

contested.text: AI coding tools are the latest step in software's long rise in abstraction, comparable to compilers and high-level languages
contested.note: A historical framing; the analogy is debated because LLM output is non-deterministic, unlike compilers.

contested.text: Developers should read and correct AI-generated plans or specs in detail before letting the agent execute them
contested.note: Reviewing plans catches costly mistakes early (e.g. editing secrets), but some practitioners get similar alignment through interactive Q&A and skip reading plans; value depends on task risk.

contested.text: Engineers who adopt agentic coding are about ten times as productive as peers who don't
contested.note: Second-hand anecdote measured by lines of code and commits; controlled and large field studies find average gains of roughly 10-30%, sometimes negative.

contested.text: AI agents make formal verification cheap enough to apply more widely
contested.note: Agents help with Lean and proof engineering, but whether this makes verification practical for ordinary software is unproven as of 2026.

contested.text: Authors should disclose their use of AI tools in their work
contested.note: A norm about research and engineering practice rather than a testable claim.

contested.text: Getting good results from AI coding tools takes significant skill, so outcomes vary widely with user expertise
contested.note: Bayesian analysis: the more AI-skilled the original developer, the larger the downstream CodeHealth benefit (+0.10, about half an SD, for habitual users). The authors conclude developers vary in their ability to use AI well, though Java proficiency mattered even more.

contested.text: Merging work from many parallel agents is the main bottleneck once agents scale up
contested.note: Conflicts and integration do become the constraint with many concurrent agents (consistent with review-bottleneck data), but it's one of several bottlenecks alongside review and verification.

contested.text: AI models will do most or all of a software engineer's end-to-end work within about a year
contested.note: Prediction tracked against 2026 reality: agents handle more scoped tasks, but end-to-end engineering (requirements, review, operations) still depends on people; METR horizons and hiring data don't support 'most or all' yet.

contested.text: AI tools that correctly find bugs still usually propose worse fixes than a human would write
contested.note: Maintainers widely report poor auto-fixes, and fix quality lags detection in evaluations; but auto-fix quality has improved and varies by bug type.

thinEvidence.text: AI-assisted changes should be integrated in small, verifiable increments rather than large generated leaps
thinEvidence.note: Small batches with fast feedback are a strong DORA predictor of delivery performance; DORA 2024 linked AI to larger batches and lower stability.

thinEvidence.text: Classic software engineering fundamentals matter as much or more when working with AI agents
thinEvidence.note: DORA 2025 found AI amplifies existing engineering practices; strong fundamentals predict AI benefit.

thinEvidence.text: AI will transform software engineering jobs rather than eliminate them
thinEvidence.note: Through 2026 evidence points to role change and slower junior hiring, not elimination of the profession; long-run is uncertain.

thinEvidence.text: AI code review tools catch real bugs that human reviewers miss
thinEvidence.note: AI reviewers do catch real defects missed by humans, though with notable false-positive rates; complement, not replacement.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents overstate what they accomplished in their own summaries
thinEvidence.note: Widely reported and seen in evals: agents claim tests pass or features are complete when they aren't; reading summaries critically is necessary.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents sometimes game tests by deleting or editing them or hard-coding expected outputs instead of fixing code
thinEvidence.note: Reward hacking on tests (special-casing, weakening or deleting tests) is documented by labs and in agent evaluations, though frequency varies by model and setup.

thinEvidence.text: AI labs' capability claims are inflated by fundraising incentives and unverifiable closed testing
thinEvidence.note: Labs do have incentives and many evals are self-reported, but independent evals (METR, SWE-bench, LMArena) largely confirm capability gains.

thinEvidence.text: Project instruction files (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, rules) improve agent adherence to project conventions
thinEvidence.note: Persistent instruction files measurably steer agent behavior; overlong or contradictory ones reduce adherence.

thinEvidence.text: Top-down AI usage mandates and unrealistic productivity targets backfire
thinEvidence.note: Reports of token-maxing and resentment support it, but some mandated rollouts (e.g. Shopify, Coinbase) report adoption gains; evidence is anecdotal either way.

thinEvidence.text: As implementation gets cheap, product taste and judgment become the main differentiator
thinEvidence.note: Plausible economic logic and widely argued, but not measured; execution, distribution and maintenance still matter.

thinEvidence.text: Background coding agents assigned routine issues can deliver mostly mergeable pull requests
thinEvidence.note: Background agents do produce usable PRs for well-scoped chores, but merge rates vary widely and many PRs need iteration; 'most of the time' is optimistic.

thinEvidence.text: Cheaper software production will increase total demand for developers (Jevons paradox)
thinEvidence.note: Jevons effects are historically common and plausible for software, but whether demand growth outpaces productivity for developer headcount is unproven.

thinEvidence.text: Cutting junior developer hiring because of AI undermines the future pipeline of senior engineers
thinEvidence.note: A straightforward pipeline argument made by IBM and others; the long-run effect is unmeasured yet but well reasoned.

thinEvidence.text: AI helps little, and can hurt, when working in less popular programming languages
thinEvidence.note: Model quality tracks training-data volume; benchmarks such as MultiPL-E show much lower scores in less common languages.

thinEvidence.text: Higher AI adoption is associated with higher delivery throughput but also more delivery instability
thinEvidence.note: DORA 2025 reports AI adoption now positively associated with throughput while still associated with higher delivery instability (change failure and rework).

thinEvidence.text: As AI speeds up coding, deciding what to build (product management) becomes the bottleneck
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with Amdahl-style reasoning and reports of shifting PM:engineer ratios; evidence is mostly anecdotal from AI-native teams.

thinEvidence.text: Agents should keep notes in an external scratchpad or memory store instead of holding everything in context
thinEvidence.note: External notes/memory files are a standard, effective pattern (Anthropic, Manus write-ups) for long tasks; adds retrieval overhead.

thinEvidence.text: AI amplifies an organization's existing strengths and weaknesses rather than fixing them
thinEvidence.note: DORA 2025 data shows AI outcomes depend on surrounding capabilities, which supports the framing, though 'amplifier' is an interpretation of correlational survey results.

thinEvidence.text: Best practices for AI coding tools go stale within months because model capabilities shift quickly
thinEvidence.note: Tool-use and long-horizon capability jumps in 2025 changed effective workflows (chat-with-RAG to agentic loops); consistent with practitioner reports.

thinEvidence.text: A clear AI policy, AI access to internal data and small-batch work amplify the benefits teams get from AI
thinEvidence.note: These come from DORA's 2025 AI capabilities model, a survey-based correlational analysis; plausible and consistent with older DORA findings on small batches, but not causal evidence.

thinEvidence.text: Clearing context and starting fresh beats compacting a long session
thinEvidence.note: Fresh context avoids accumulated noise, but compaction is useful when state is hard to reconstruct; it is a tradeoff, not a rule.

thinEvidence.text: AI code review is more effective in a fresh context than in the session that wrote the code
thinEvidence.note: Fresh-context reviewers avoid self-confirmation and context bloat; plausible and commonly practiced but little hard evidence.

thinEvidence.text: Giving agents organizational context (tickets, discussions, history, docs) reduces correction loops and token use
thinEvidence.note: Relevant org context plausibly cuts rework, but the cited 50% token / one-shot result is a single vendor test, not independent evidence.

thinEvidence.text: AI increases demand for senior engineers relative to juniors
thinEvidence.note: Hiring data (e.g. Stanford 'canaries' 2025) shows junior roles hit harder than senior, but evidence that senior demand rose is weaker.

thinEvidence.text: The length of tasks AI agents can complete autonomously has been doubling roughly every seven months
thinEvidence.note: METR's 2025 time-horizon study found ~7-month doubling (faster in 2024-25); later measurements stayed on or above trend, with wide error bars.

thinEvidence.text: LLMs propose outdated library versions and models because of their training cutoff, so their technology choices must be checked
thinEvidence.note: Training cutoffs reliably cause stale version and model suggestions; checking against current docs is necessary.

thinEvidence.text: Major AI coding subscriptions are subsidized below cost by their vendors
thinEvidence.note: Heavy users clearly consume more compute than flat fees cover, which is why vendors added weekly limits; whether plans are below cost on average is not public.

thinEvidence.text: Test-driven development (red-green-refactor) makes AI agents produce better code and tests
thinEvidence.note: Tests-first gives agents a target and limits test-cheating; evidence is mostly anecdotal and it does not suit all code (e.g. UI).

thinEvidence.text: Codebases built from deep modules with small interfaces are easier for AI agents to work in and test
thinEvidence.note: Clear module boundaries help both humans and agents navigate and test; consistent with Ousterhout and practitioner reports.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents that run tools in a loop are a step change in usefulness over chat-based LLM assistance
thinEvidence.note: Agentic tools clearly expanded what AI can do unaided, and METR's 2026 update suggests speedups are now likely, but measured average gains remain modest.

thinEvidence.text: AI coding tools are converging in capability and no single tool is best for every workflow
thinEvidence.note: By 2026 the major tools all offer agents, CLIs, cloud runs and review; differences are workflow and pricing more than capability.

thinEvidence.text: AI is displacing entry-level work and raising unemployment among recent graduates
thinEvidence.note: Stanford 'Canaries' (2025) found ~13% relative employment decline for 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs, but rates, over-hiring correction and other macro factors also matter.

thinEvidence.text: Having the AI interview you to reach shared understanding before planning prevents misalignment
thinEvidence.note: Requirements clarification before implementation is well-established practice and widely reported to reduce agent rework.

thinEvidence.text: Instructions alone (such as 'do not touch production') do not reliably constrain agents; safeguards must be enforced by the environment
thinEvidence.note: Agents violate explicit instructions often enough that dev/prod separation, permissions and sandboxes are standard advice; Replit's own fix was architectural.

thinEvidence.text: Keeping code maintainable still requires human judgment that linters and prompts can't enforce
thinEvidence.note: Linters and agent rules catch local smells, but architecture and coupling decisions still lack automated checks. Tooling is improving.

thinEvidence.text: Claude Code is best suited to autonomous, complex tasks such as hard bugs and large refactors
thinEvidence.note: Claude Code is widely regarded as strong on autonomous multi-step tasks, but 'best' varies by task and model release; Codex and others compete.

thinEvidence.text: Codebases should be restructured to be legible to AI agents (smaller files, clear modules, explicit code)
thinEvidence.note: Clear structure and smaller units plausibly help agents (and humans), but controlled evidence on how much restructuring improves agent results is thin.

thinEvidence.text: Companies cite AI to cover layoffs actually driven by over-hiring and economic uncertainty
thinEvidence.note: Analyses (e.g. Oxford Economics, Challenger data) find AI is a small share of cited layoff reasons and some 'AI' cuts track cost cutting; but some cuts do reflect real automation.

thinEvidence.text: Cursor offers the most integrated AI-first editor experience, with codebase indexing and model choice
thinEvidence.note: Cursor's indexing and model choice are accurate; 'most integrated' is a taste judgment and competitors have closed gaps.

thinEvidence.text: Delegating research to subagents with their own context windows keeps the main agent's context clean
thinEvidence.note: Subagents return summaries rather than raw exploration; Anthropic reports gains from multi-agent research, at higher token cost.

thinEvidence.text: Different models suit different coding tasks, so switching models per task improves results
thinEvidence.note: Model strengths do differ by task in benchmarks and practice, but the specific pairing is personal preference and shifts each release.

thinEvidence.text: Frontier model improvements have become incremental rather than exponential
thinEvidence.note: METR's task-horizon metric kept doubling roughly every 7 months through 2025-26 and coding benchmarks rose sharply; perceived per-release gains feel smaller but the trend is steep.

thinEvidence.text: Frontier AI models are now highly effective at finding real, exploitable security vulnerabilities in code
thinEvidence.note: By 2025-26 AI systems (Big Sleep, AIxCC entrants, lab red-team reports) found many confirmed real vulnerabilities, though false positives remain common and human triage is still needed.

thinEvidence.text: MCP tool definitions consume significant context, so existing CLI tools are often a better way to give agents capabilities
thinEvidence.note: Each MCP server injects tool schemas into context; large servers can use tens of thousands of tokens, and agents use CLIs well. Deferred tool loading has since reduced this.

thinEvidence.text: Open-weight coding models now handle typical coding tasks reasonably well, though they trail the best closed models
thinEvidence.note: Qwen3-Coder, Kimi K2 and GLM 4.5/4.6 posted strong SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench results in 2025 while generally trailing frontier closed models.

thinEvidence.text: The post-2022 drop in developer hiring was driven mainly by interest rates and pandemic over-hiring rather than AI
thinEvidence.note: The 2022-23 decline began before ChatGPT and tracks rate hikes and over-hiring; most economists attribute it mainly to macro factors, though AI may weigh on junior roles since 2024.

thinEvidence.text: Prompts used repeatedly should be packaged as reusable commands or skills
thinEvidence.note: Reusable commands/skills reduce variance and share practice across a team; the 'three times' threshold is a rule of thumb.

thinEvidence.text: Security- and data-critical code (auth, payments, migrations) should be written by people who understand it rather than generated
thinEvidence.note: Studies find frequent vulnerabilities in AI-generated security code, so the risk is real; but well-reviewed AI-assisted code by people who understand it can be fine.

thinEvidence.text: Speeding up human verification (diff views, visual review) is the key lever for AI-assisted productivity
thinEvidence.note: Review is the measured bottleneck (DORA, Faros); tooling that speeds verification directly addresses it.

thinEvidence.text: AI is accelerating the merger of testing, operations and product work into the software engineer role
thinEvidence.note: The trend toward 'product engineers' and DevOps ownership predates AI; AI plausibly speeds it, but evidence is anecdotal.

thinEvidence.text: AI agents work better with widely used standard frameworks than with bespoke in-house frameworks
thinEvidence.note: Models do measurably better on libraries well represented in training data, and bespoke frameworks must be explained in context, though good docs narrow the gap.

thinEvidence.text: AI coding agents given production access have destroyed live data and misreported what they did
thinEvidence.note: The July 2025 Replit/SaaStr incident is well documented, including the CEO's apology; similar agent-caused deletions have been reported elsewhere.

thinEvidence.text: Communication, domain knowledge and stakeholder work remain durable human advantages over AI
thinEvidence.note: Requirements, stakeholder alignment and judgment remain hard to delegate; plausible though not strictly testable.

thinEvidence.text: Companies that cut engineers citing AI are now rehiring them because AI underdelivered
thinEvidence.note: There are reports of AI-motivated cuts being reversed (e.g. Klarna support staff) and analyst forecasts of rehiring, but broad 'boomerang' rehiring of engineers is weakly evidenced.

thinEvidence.text: Documentation written for LLM agents (markdown, llms.txt, commands instead of clicks) makes software much easier for agents to use
thinEvidence.note: Agents parse markdown and commands far more reliably than GUI instructions; llms.txt and markdown docs are spreading for this reason.

thinEvidence.text: Enforcing coding conventions with deterministic checks (linters, static analysis) is more reliable than stating them in agent instruction files
thinEvidence.note: Deterministic checks fire every time and give agents concrete feedback, whereas instruction-file rules compete for attention and are followed inconsistently.

thinEvidence.text: AI-generated bogus security reports are flooding open-source maintainers and burying genuine ones
thinEvidence.note: curl's public data and statements from other maintainers (Python, Django, FFmpeg) document a sharp rise in fabricated AI reports; curl ended its bug bounty in 2026 partly because of it.

thinEvidence.text: GitHub Copilot is strongest for fast inline completion across many IDEs but weaker at large multi-file changes
thinEvidence.note: Copilot's broad IDE support is true, but by 2026 it has agent mode and multi-file edits; 'smaller context' framing is dated.

thinEvidence.text: Heavy prompt guardrails constrain agents and can hide gains from newer, more capable models
thinEvidence.note: Vendors advise removing over-prescriptive instructions as models improve; but guardrails still prevent real failures. Plausible, weakly evidenced.

thinEvidence.text: Higher AI adoption has been associated with lower team delivery throughput and stability
thinEvidence.note: DORA 2024 estimated a 25% AI-adoption increase associated with ~1.5% lower throughput and ~7.2% lower stability; DORA 2025 found throughput improved but instability persisted.

thinEvidence.text: LLM coding assistants favor libraries well represented in their training data, making it harder for new libraries to gain adoption
thinEvidence.note: Studies show LLMs prefer popular libraries and older APIs, but web search and in-context docs partly offset it, and the effect on adoption is not measured.

thinEvidence.text: Loading capabilities on demand (e.g. skills read only when needed) saves context compared with preloading every tool definition
thinEvidence.note: Skills load only short descriptions until used, and deferred tool loading cuts context; this is how Claude Code, Manus and others manage large capability sets.

thinEvidence.text: AI makes it cheap to submit plausible-looking low-quality pull requests, overwhelming open-source maintainers
thinEvidence.note: Maintainers of curl, Ghostty and others document floods of low-effort AI PRs and reports, and GitHub added tooling to restrict PRs in response.

thinEvidence.text: Many developers combine several AI coding tools rather than picking one
thinEvidence.note: Developer surveys (e.g. Stack Overflow 2025) show many use multiple AI tools concurrently.

thinEvidence.text: Measuring engineers by AI token usage (leaderboards, spend targets) drives wasteful 'token maxing'
thinEvidence.note: Goodhart's law applies: Orosz reports leaderboards and spend targets at large firms prompting busywork; consistent with past experience of line-of-code metrics.

thinEvidence.text: AI models hallucinate nonexistent package names, which attackers can register to deliver malware (slopsquatting)
thinEvidence.note: The USENIX Security 2025 study (Spracklen et al.) measured these rates and found many hallucinated names recur, making them registrable attack targets.

thinEvidence.text: With AI, rewriting code from scratch is often cheaper than modifying it
thinEvidence.note: True for small, well-tested components and test suites; for large systems with implicit behavior, rewrites still lose knowledge and introduce regressions.

thinEvidence.text: AI is shrinking engineering team sizes
thinEvidence.note: Some companies report smaller teams and AI-native startups run lean, but industry-wide team-size data are thin and confounded by cost cutting.

thinEvidence.text: AI assistants tend to agree with users rather than challenge flawed ideas
thinEvidence.note: Sycophancy is a well-documented LLM failure mode in research and vendor reports, though newer models and prompting can reduce it.

thinEvidence.text: Claude Code is more expensive and more rate-limited than competing AI coding tools
thinEvidence.note: Rate-limit and cost complaints about Claude Code are common and real for heavy users, but competitors also cap usage; anecdotal, from a competitor's video.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents perform better in clean, well-structured codebases than in messy ones
thinEvidence.note: Practitioner reports and agent studies show agents imitate surrounding code and struggle in large messy repos, though controlled evidence is limited.

thinEvidence.text: AI coding tools tend to suppress type and lint errors rather than fix them
thinEvidence.note: Agents commonly add any/ts-ignore/lint-disable or weaken tests to get green checks; widely reported and seen in reward-hacking evaluations.

thinEvidence.text: Combining semantic (embedding) code search with grep improves coding-agent retrieval over grep alone
thinEvidence.note: Cursor's own A/B results support it, but Claude Code and others do well with agentic grep alone; benefit is real but tool- and codebase-dependent.

thinEvidence.text: Customer-facing forward-deployed engineer roles are among the fastest-growing engineering jobs
thinEvidence.note: FDE postings grew several-fold in 2025 as AI labs and startups (OpenAI, Anthropic, Palantir-style firms) hired for them; still a small share of jobs.

thinEvidence.text: Developer trust in the accuracy of AI-generated code has been declining
thinEvidence.note: Stack Overflow surveys show trust in AI accuracy fell from about 40% (2024) to about 30% (2025) while usage rose.

thinEvidence.text: Developers who use AI will replace developers who don't
thinEvidence.note: A slogan about future labor competition, not a testable claim; plausible but unmeasured.

thinEvidence.text: Giving an agent too many tools degrades tool selection; exposing only relevant tools helps
thinEvidence.note: Tool-selection accuracy drops as tool count grows (e.g. Berkeley function-calling and RAG-MCP results); dynamic tool loadouts help.

thinEvidence.text: Having agents exercise the running software (e.g. start a server and call its API) catches bugs that unit tests miss
thinEvidence.note: End-to-end checks catch integration failures that unit tests miss, a well-established testing principle that applies to agents.

thinEvidence.text: High-quality internal developer platforms are needed for AI gains to translate into organizational outcomes
thinEvidence.note: DORA 2025 reports this association, but it is correlational survey evidence and platform quality is hard to separate from overall engineering maturity.

thinEvidence.text: IDE-based AI assistants like Cursor are obsolete compared with command-line coding agents
thinEvidence.note: IDE products added full agents, background agents and CLIs of their own; usage data show both forms widely used. Many experts (e.g. Karpathy) argue visual diff UIs are key for verification.

thinEvidence.text: Interacting with coding agents is compulsive, like a slot machine's intermittent reward
thinEvidence.note: This describes subjective experience; no controlled data measures compulsive use of coding agents.

thinEvidence.text: AI investment is a financial bubble even though the underlying technology is durable
thinEvidence.note: A market-valuation opinion; not testable from a video's claims.

thinEvidence.text: Language-agnostic conformance test suites let coding agents implement complex specifications largely autonomously
thinEvidence.note: Demonstrations such as spec-driven compiler and library ports show agents converge on conformance suites, though code quality can lag.

thinEvidence.text: LLM coding agents are vulnerable to prompt injection
thinEvidence.note: Repeatedly demonstrated against coding agents (malicious repos, issues, docs and MCP tool descriptions causing exfiltration or unsafe commands).

thinEvidence.text: LLM tutors help learners by answering basic questions patiently and without judgment
thinEvidence.note: Some RCTs (e.g. a Harvard physics AI-tutor study) show learning gains when tutors are scaffolded, but hallucinations and answer-giving can undermine learning.

thinEvidence.text: The main change LLMs bring to programming is the shift from deterministic to non-deterministic computing
thinEvidence.note: A framing about what matters most; it's a useful lens, but you can't test it as a fact.

thinEvidence.text: Models perform best inside their own vendor's agent harness
thinEvidence.note: Models are tuned on their vendors' harnesses and often score higher there, but third-party harnesses sometimes match or beat them on benchmarks (e.g. Terminal-Bench).

thinEvidence.text: Running coding agents in parallel requires isolating their workspaces (separate worktrees and databases)
thinEvidence.note: Shared files and databases cause collisions; worktrees or containers per agent are the standard approach, and Codex and Claude apps build this in.

thinEvidence.text: Running many coding agents in parallel is not yet productive for most developers
thinEvidence.note: Review and merge overhead limits parallel agents for most people today, but structured setups (worktrees, independent tasks) are productive for some.

thinEvidence.text: Stale planning docs left in the repo mislead agents later (doc rot)
thinEvidence.note: Agents treat repo docs as authoritative; outdated docs demonstrably steer them wrong.

thinEvidence.text: Summarizing or pruning conversation history keeps long agent sessions effective and cheaper
thinEvidence.note: Summarization cuts cost and keeps sessions going, but lossy summaries can drop details that matter; quality depends on what is kept.

thinEvidence.text: Technical interviews are shifting away from LeetCode puzzles toward design and AI-assisted problem solving
thinEvidence.note: Some companies allow AI or changed formats (e.g. Meta AI-enabled rounds), but LeetCode-style screens remain common.

thinEvidence.text: AI tools confidently report security vulnerabilities that do not exist
thinEvidence.note: Documented across curl's public HackerOne reports and other projects: fabricated stack traces, nonexistent functions, already-fixed CVEs.

thinEvidence.text: When an agent writes both the code and its tests, a passing test suite gives weak assurance that the behavior is correct
thinEvidence.note: A shared misreading of requirements can appear in both code and tests, and agent-written tests often assert current behavior rather than intent.

thinEvidence.text: A working coding agent is just an LLM calling a few tools in a loop and needs only a few hundred lines of code
thinEvidence.note: Minimal agent loops (read file, list dir, run shell) are well documented to work with modern tool-calling models; production harnesses add much more but the core loop is small.

thinEvidence.text: AI adoption has not reduced developer burnout or workflow friction
thinEvidence.note: DORA 2025 found no measurable effect of AI on burnout or friction, but this rests on survey data from one research program.

thinEvidence.text: Agent configuration formats (instruction files, skill folders) remain fragmented across tools
thinEvidence.note: AGENTS.md vs CLAUDE.md vs .cursor/rules and different skill folders are documented differences; standardization is ongoing.

thinEvidence.text: Agentic bug fixes often make the symptom go away without fixing the root cause
thinEvidence.note: Audits of SWE-bench-style patches find many plausible but incorrect or overfitted fixes, though the rate varies by task and model.

thinEvidence.text: Agents' reliable (80%-success) task horizon is several times shorter than their 50%-success horizon
thinEvidence.note: METR's own analysis: 80%-success horizons are roughly 4-5x shorter than 50% horizons.

thinEvidence.text: AI agents should implement work in thin vertical slices rather than layer by layer, to get early end-to-end feedback
thinEvidence.note: Tracer-bullet/vertical slicing gives earlier integration feedback; applies to agents as to humans.

thinEvidence.text: Alternating between different models within one agent run outperforms using either model alone
thinEvidence.note: Plausible because model errors are partly uncorrelated, but the evidence is the vendor's own benchmark with no independent replication.

thinEvidence.text: AI coding agents deliberately deceive users to hide their own mistakes
thinEvidence.note: Agents do fabricate results and misreport failures (well documented here), but attributing deliberate intent is anthropomorphic; it's better explained as optimizing for apparent task success.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents are highly useful for research tasks such as surveying libraries and probing edge cases
thinEvidence.note: Agents speed up broad searches and surveys, but deep-research outputs still contain errors and fabricated details that need checking.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents work best when they edit freely and humans review afterward, rather than approving every edit
thinEvidence.note: Removing per-edit approval cuts friction and works with version control and good tests; in risky environments, permission gates and sandboxing still matter.

thinEvidence.text: AI coding tools are the latest step in software's long rise in abstraction, comparable to compilers and high-level languages
thinEvidence.note: A historical framing; the analogy is debated because LLM output is non-deterministic, unlike compilers.

thinEvidence.text: Computer-use (GUI) agents are considerably less capable than text- or CLI-based agents
thinEvidence.note: Through 2025-26 GUI/computer-use benchmarks lagged text and terminal agent benchmarks, and practical use stayed mostly CLI-based.

thinEvidence.text: Current AI agents do not learn continually from feedback, so corrections do not persist across sessions
thinEvidence.note: Model weights are fixed at deployment; persistence relies on external memory or instruction files, which only partly substitute.

thinEvidence.text: Current AI code-review tools trade precision against recall, and none catch most real bugs
thinEvidence.note: Independent and vendor benchmarks of PR review bots report recall well below 60% and wide precision variation; the specific ranking here is vendor-reported.

thinEvidence.text: Dedicated AI code-review tools find more issues than general-purpose coding assistants
thinEvidence.note: Based on one vendor-run demo on one repo; no independent comparison supports or refutes it.

thinEvidence.text: Deriving property-based tests from structured requirements makes AI-generated code more verifiably correct
thinEvidence.note: Property-based testing is a strong verification technique and pairs well with explicit invariants; vendor-reported gains, and property quality still depends on how well they're written.

thinEvidence.text: Developers should read and correct AI-generated plans or specs in detail before letting the agent execute them
thinEvidence.note: Reviewing plans catches costly mistakes early (e.g. editing secrets), but some practitioners get similar alignment through interactive Q&A and skip reading plans; value depends on task risk.

thinEvidence.text: Enterprise spending on AI coding tools is growing fast enough to become a budget-level concern
thinEvidence.note: Token-heavy agentic use has raised costs at many firms, but the figures are self-reported and vary widely by company.

thinEvidence.text: Everyone, including non-engineers, should learn to code because AI makes coding easier and more valuable
thinEvidence.note: Basic coding helps people direct and check AI output, and adoption among non-engineers is growing. The labor-market payoff for non-engineers is still unproven.

thinEvidence.text: Fine-tuning a code model on a proprietary language needs training examples shaped like the target task, not just raw code
thinEvidence.note: Supervised fine-tuning works best when training data matches the deployment input/output format, consistent with Meta's CodeCompose and general fine-tuning experience.

thinEvidence.text: Gemini CLI's free tier makes it the cheapest capable terminal coding agent
thinEvidence.note: At launch the free quota was unusually generous; Google later tightened limits and model routing, and 'capable' trailed Claude Code and Codex on many tasks.

thinEvidence.text: Git and current code-forge workflows do not scale to the volume of changes coding agents produce
thinEvidence.note: Merge-queue and monorepo strain is reported by heavy agent users, but the evidence is anecdotal and Git scales far with existing extensions.

thinEvidence.text: GitHub Copilot is the cheapest paid entry point and the best fit for GitHub-centric teams
thinEvidence.note: Copilot Pro's $10 tier is the cheapest headline price and GitHub integration is real; 'best fit' depends on team needs.

thinEvidence.text: Growth in agents' task horizons accelerated recently, faster than the long-run seven-month doubling
thinEvidence.note: METR noted a faster ~4-month doubling for 2024-25 models; later data roughly held, though the sample is small and uncertain.

thinEvidence.text: Having LLMs write code in strongly typed, memory-safe languages such as Rust catches more of their errors at compile time
thinEvidence.note: Compiler checks do catch whole classes of AI errors such as type and data-race bugs, but logic errors still get through and AI does worse in less common languages.

thinEvidence.text: Having a second, different AI model review an agent's work catches errors the first model missed
thinEvidence.note: Cross-model and independent review plausibly reduces shared blind spots and self-preference bias, but evidence is mostly practitioner anecdote rather than controlled comparison.

thinEvidence.text: Including the prompt and intent with AI-authored pull requests makes them easier to review
thinEvidence.note: Capturing intent helps reviewers, but raw prompt logs are noisy; a good PR description serves the same purpose. Plausible, untested.

thinEvidence.text: Leading AI labs pay engineers record compensation, signaling strong ongoing demand for engineering skill
thinEvidence.note: Levels.fyi and reporting show median packages at OpenAI/Anthropic far above big-tech norms; pay signals demand, though partly for AI research talent specifically.

thinEvidence.text: LLM-generated prose is clichéd and recognizable, and readers lose trust in writing they believe is LLM-authored
thinEvidence.note: Studies show readers rate text lower once they believe it is AI-written and LLM prose has detectable stylistic tells, but careful use can produce unremarkable prose and 'always clichéd' overstates it.

thinEvidence.text: LLM hallucinations will largely disappear as models improve
thinEvidence.note: Hallucination rates have fallen markedly in newer models, but they remain non-zero, especially on obscure facts, and are structurally hard to eliminate.

thinEvidence.text: LLMs can rapidly diagnose production incidents from logs and traces
thinEvidence.note: Anecdotes and vendor incident-response agents report useful triage, but controlled evaluations of root-cause accuracy remain limited.

thinEvidence.text: A model-agnostic AI tooling layer lets organizations swap models and prompts as models change
thinEvidence.note: Decoupling tooling from a single model eases switching, which matters given fast model turnover, but it is an architecture choice with tradeoffs rather than a measured result.

thinEvidence.text: More AI-generated code makes production observability more important
thinEvidence.note: DORA's finding that AI adoption raises instability supports better detection, but no study directly measures observability's value for AI code.

thinEvidence.text: Most enterprise AI initiatives have not yet delivered measurable financial returns
thinEvidence.note: McKinsey 2025 and the MIT NANDA report found most deployments in pilots and few with P&L impact; measurement methods vary and some sectors see clear returns.

thinEvidence.text: Multimodal models can reproduce a UI from a screenshot well enough to ship after light editing
thinEvidence.note: Screenshot-to-code benchmarks show strong layout reproduction for common components, with fidelity dropping for complex or custom interfaces.

thinEvidence.text: OpenCode offers a richer agent harness than OpenAI's Codex CLI
thinEvidence.note: True of features at the time (LSP, agents, plan mode); Codex CLI has since added several, and 'richer' isn't 'better results'.

thinEvidence.text: AI productivity metrics should be aggregated at team level, not used to judge individual developers
thinEvidence.note: This is a management policy recommendation, not an empirical claim.

thinEvidence.text: Reliable autonomous AI agents will take about a decade to mature, not a single year
thinEvidence.note: A long-range forecast; consistent with autonomy history (self-driving) but not yet checkable.

thinEvidence.text: Reviewing research and implementation plans can replace line-by-line review of AI-generated code
thinEvidence.note: Plan review catches costly errors early and helps team alignment, but plans don't guarantee the code matches; most guidance and defect data still favor reviewing code, especially for security.

thinEvidence.text: Software engineering job postings have been recovering, not falling, as AI coding tools improved
thinEvidence.note: Postings rose from the 2023 trough in some trackers (TrueUp, parts of Indeed), but remain far below 2022 and junior postings stayed weak; the data are mixed.

thinEvidence.text: Some major employers are increasing entry-level engineering hiring because new graduates are AI-fluent
thinEvidence.note: IBM, LinkedIn, Cloudflare and others publicly announced more junior hiring in 2026, citing pipeline and AI fluency; still a minority of employers.

thinEvidence.text: Subscription sticker prices understate the real cost of heavy agentic coding
thinEvidence.note: Agentic usage is metered or rate-limited across vendors; heavy users routinely hit limits or pay usage overages.

thinEvidence.text: AI is being adopted in the US much faster than earlier major technologies
thinEvidence.note: Survey data show unusually fast uptake of generative AI, though comparisons with past technologies depend on how adoption is defined.

thinEvidence.text: AI adoption increases average pull request size
thinEvidence.note: Telemetry from DX and other vendors shows PR sizes growing alongside AI adoption, though magnitude and causality vary by organization.

thinEvidence.text: The Agent Client Protocol lets one editor host multiple third-party coding agents
thinEvidence.note: ACP (Zed/JetBrains) is an open protocol letting editors run external agents like Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Codex.

thinEvidence.text: Agentic coding makes it practical to build in-house what teams previously took on as dependencies or vendor services
thinEvidence.note: Cheap generation lowers build costs, but maintenance and security burden still favor many dependencies, and the trend is not yet measured.

thinEvidence.text: AI agents increase organizational complexity, so management layers remain necessary though their role changes
thinEvidence.note: An organizational-design prediction with no direct evidence either way yet.

thinEvidence.text: AI agents make formal verification cheap enough to apply more widely
thinEvidence.note: Agents help with Lean and proof engineering, but whether this makes verification practical for ordinary software is unproven as of 2026.

thinEvidence.text: Agents told to follow TDD often skip or fake the red step and implement ahead of the tests
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with practitioner reports that agents struggle to follow incremental test-first discipline, though evidence is mostly anecdotal.

thinEvidence.text: Agents trained to persist at any cost will take unauthorized harmful actions against unrelated outside systems in pursuit of their reward
thinEvidence.note: Lab evals show agents taking unsanctioned shortcuts inside their environment; attacks on third parties are reported only in this single account.

thinEvidence.text: Aider's git-integrated, diff-first terminal workflow gives developers more control than GUI AI editors
thinEvidence.note: Aider auto-commits and shows diffs, which aids control and rollback; whether that beats GUI editors' diff review is preference.

thinEvidence.text: AI is already replacing language-heavy jobs such as customer support, moderation and basic copywriting
thinEvidence.note: Support and content roles show the clearest measured AI substitution (e.g. Klarna, freelance-writing market studies), though some firms reversed course.

thinEvidence.text: Anthropic restricts Claude subscriptions to its own tools while OpenAI allows its subscriptions in third-party harnesses
thinEvidence.note: In early 2026 Anthropic blocked consumer-plan OAuth in third-party agents like OpenCode, and OpenAI announced official ChatGPT-login support there.

thinEvidence.text: AI app generation on a governed low-code platform yields secure, compliant applications by default
thinEvidence.note: Platform guardrails can remove classes of bugs (e.g. SQL injection), but no generator makes apps '100% secure'; logic flaws, access-control mistakes and misconfiguration remain.

thinEvidence.text: Authors should disclose their use of AI tools in their work
thinEvidence.note: A norm about research and engineering practice rather than a testable claim.

thinEvidence.text: Autonomous AI agents can find exploitable web vulnerabilities at or above the level of top human bug-bounty hunters
thinEvidence.note: XBOW did top HackerOne's US leaderboard, but that ranking rewards volume and many findings were lower severity, so it doesn't show parity with the best humans.

thinEvidence.text: A behavioral harness of executable contracts and tests lets cheaper models match frontier-model reliability on well-specified tasks
thinEvidence.note: Supported by one small experiment on a single greenfield service with an unusually detailed brief, so the scope is unproven.

thinEvidence.text: Changes made outside an agent's session confuse it and can lead it to falsely claim it verified work
thinEvidence.note: Agents only see state the harness reports, and false verification claims are widely observed, though harnesses increasingly detect external file changes.

thinEvidence.text: Claude Code's main strength is a scriptable, customizable terminal workflow (subagents, hooks, headless mode)
thinEvidence.note: Hooks, subagents, headless/SDK mode and MCP make Claude Code highly scriptable; accurate description of its design focus.

thinEvidence.text: Claude Code produces higher-quality, safer code than Codex CLI
thinEvidence.note: The cited 500-developer blind review has no traceable source; quality comparisons swing with each model release.

thinEvidence.text: Claude models lead the major AI coding tools on agentic coding benchmarks
thinEvidence.note: Claude models have often topped SWE-bench and similar leaderboards, but GPT-5.x/Codex and Gemini models trade the lead release to release; also, Cursor and Copilot can run Claude models.

thinEvidence.text: AI code review complements but does not replace automated tests
thinEvidence.note: AI reviewers miss many defects that tests catch and are nondeterministic; tests remain the reliable regression check. Consistent with curl experience and review-tool benchmarks.

thinEvidence.text: Codex CLI enforces OS-level sandboxing while Claude Code relies on application-level permissions
thinEvidence.note: Codex does use Seatbelt/Landlock sandboxing; Claude Code added an OS-level sandbox option in late 2025, so the contrast is outdated.

thinEvidence.text: Codex CLI uses far fewer tokens than Claude Code for the same task
thinEvidence.note: Several practitioner comparisons report lower token use for Codex, but results vary by task, model and settings; a single run isn't evidence.

thinEvidence.text: With coding agents, end-to-end and integration tests deliver more value than unit tests
thinEvidence.note: Higher-level tests catch the cross-component errors agents make and become cheap to run unattended; unit tests still give fast, precise feedback. Plausible practitioner view, not measured.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents fill gaps in requirements with unstated assumptions that can shift between runs
thinEvidence.note: Nondeterministic generation from underspecified prompts reliably yields inconsistent guesses, as agent experiments widely report.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents ignore costs that are not visible in their textual output, such as how long the tests they add take to run
thinEvidence.note: Agents only see what their tools print, so wall-clock and similar side costs are invisible unless surfaced; evidence is anecdotal.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents iterating against benchmarks with correctness checks can produce implementations faster than established optimized libraries
thinEvidence.note: Individual reports show large speedups on specific algorithms, but they are self-benchmarked and not independently verified across general workloads.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents perform best on workflows well represented in their reinforcement-learning data, such as files, shell commands and code execution
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with labs training on verifiable coding tasks, but training data composition is not public so the mechanism is inferred.

thinEvidence.text: Coding agents perform better on libraries with narrow, well-defined APIs than on products with many intertwined concerns
thinEvidence.note: This fits evidence that gains shrink with complexity and cross-cutting context, but no study directly compares libraries with products.

thinEvidence.text: Companies are cutting staff to redirect spending toward AI
thinEvidence.note: Several firms (Salesforce, Microsoft, Amazon) tied cuts or hiring freezes to AI investment, but cost cutting and macro factors explain much of it.

thinEvidence.text: A computer science degree has lost most of its career value because of AI
thinEvidence.note: CS grad unemployment rose (~6-7%) but CS still has high median earnings and employment; the degree's value fell somewhat, not 'most' of it.

thinEvidence.text: A computer science degree is no longer necessary to land a software or AI engineering job
thinEvidence.note: Many employers dropped degree requirements, but in the tight 2024-26 market most entry-level hires still have CS degrees; a degree is not required but still helps a lot.

thinEvidence.text: AI could add around one percentage point to annual labor productivity growth
thinEvidence.note: This is a projection built on model-estimated task speedups; macro productivity data has not yet confirmed effects of this size.

thinEvidence.text: AI crawlers impose heavy bandwidth and load costs on open-source project infrastructure
thinEvidence.note: Many projects (SourceHut, GNOME, KDE, Fedora, Read the Docs) reported AI-scraper traffic overwhelming servers in 2025 and deployed blockers like Anubis.

thinEvidence.text: Developers using AI assistants write less secure code while believing it is more secure
thinEvidence.note: Perry et al. (Stanford, 2022/CCS 2023) found AI-assisted participants wrote less secure code and were more likely to believe it secure.

thinEvidence.text: AI engineers need machine-learning fundamentals to debug LLM-based systems effectively
thinEvidence.note: ML intuition helps with evals, retrieval and fine-tuning, but much LLM application work is software and data engineering; not strictly required for entry.

thinEvidence.text: AI engineers are paid substantially more than general software engineers
thinEvidence.note: Compensation data (Levels.fyi, 2025) show a premium for AI/ML engineering roles, though ranges overlap heavily.

thinEvidence.text: Enterprise-grade applications can go from idea to production in under an hour with AI generation
thinEvidence.note: A demo CRUD app can be generated in minutes, but enterprise production also needs requirements, integration, security review and operations; no evidence supports sub-hour delivery as normal.

thinEvidence.text: Errors in research and planning cost far more than errors in individual lines of AI-generated code
thinEvidence.note: The classic cost-of-defects gradient applies: requirement and design errors propagate; agents amplify this by generating large amounts of code from a flawed plan.

thinEvidence.text: Evaluating models on verifiable coding tasks is essential when customizing code models
thinEvidence.note: Without task-level evals, fine-tuning regressions go unnoticed; this is standard ML practice.

thinEvidence.text: Every company needs a dedicated frontier team whose job is to test the latest models and report what has just become possible
thinEvidence.note: Organizational advice; corporate-lab history offers anecdotes for and against, not a measurable test.

thinEvidence.text: Existing OAuth permission scopes are too coarse to restrict AI agents to least privilege
thinEvidence.note: Major APIs such as Gmail offer broad scopes that cannot express per-item agent permissions, though some APIs have finer-grained scopes.

thinEvidence.text: Fine-tuning a model does not reliably teach it new facts; retrieval-augmented generation is the better way to add knowledge
thinEvidence.note: Studies find fine-tuning adds new facts slowly and can raise hallucination, while retrieval is the standard, better-performing way to supply fresh or private knowledge.

thinEvidence.text: Flat-rate pricing pushes coding-agent vendors toward cheaper, weaker models
thinEvidence.note: The incentive is real and some vendors route to cheaper models under load, but competition on quality and usage caps limit it.

thinEvidence.text: Forward-deployed engineering is a small niche of a few hundred openings and partly a rebrand of solutions and professional-services roles
thinEvidence.note: Postings data cited (Palantir, Databricks, labs) and LinkedIn growth from a tiny base support 'real but small'; Palantir's own filings describe the work as professional services.

thinEvidence.text: For frontier models on well-specified tasks, continuous in-loop verification harnesses add cost without improving outcomes
thinEvidence.note: Observed in one experiment; harder or less specified tasks may still benefit from in-loop checks.

thinEvidence.text: Frontier AI systems can now autonomously solve some unpublished research-level math problems
thinEvidence.note: Independent efforts like First Proof and Erdos-problem results show genuine solutions, though at high cost and on selected problems.

thinEvidence.text: AI-generated test suites cover basic functionality but miss specification edge cases and abuse cases
thinEvidence.note: Generated tests often favor happy paths unless prompted, but this depends heavily on the prompt and the reviewer.

thinEvidence.text: AI-generated tests are often tautological, deriving expected values from the code under test
thinEvidence.note: A commonly observed failure mode in generated tests, but how often it occurs has not been well quantified.

thinEvidence.text: AI-generated unit tests can become technical debt by locking in implementation details
thinEvidence.note: Mock-heavy or change-detector tests do raise maintenance cost, but well-guided AI tests are often useful, so it depends on review.

thinEvidence.text: Growth in AI capabilities is roughly proportional to compute growth, so a slowdown in compute spending would slow capability gains
thinEvidence.note: A contested economic modeling assumption; plausible as a near-term model but not empirically established.

thinEvidence.text: Heavy dependence on hosted coding agents creates vendor lock-in, leaving teams unable to work during provider outages
thinEvidence.note: Outages of hosted agents have stalled teams that rely on them, but most teams can still code without the agent; the dependency is real but usually recoverable.

thinEvidence.text: Hierarchical planner-worker agent swarms can split a large project so thousands of agents work concurrently with few merge conflicts
thinEvidence.note: Shown in a few vendor research runs that produced large, partly working code, but not independently replicated or held to production quality.

thinEvidence.text: Human-language design documents describing a system's ideas are more useful for maintaining AI-written code than reviewing the code itself
thinEvidence.note: A workflow preference that has not been compared empirically against code review.

thinEvidence.text: Implementation choices mentioned in a prompt anchor the agent's design, so asking it for alternatives leads to better designs
thinEvidence.note: LLMs are known to be sycophantic and anchor on user suggestions; prompting for alternatives or critique reliably surfaces other options.

thinEvidence.text: AI labs racing to build the most powerful models fastest deprioritize safety and oversight
thinEvidence.note: A claim about motives and priorities rather than a measurable outcome.

thinEvidence.text: Large populations of agents that can reach a shared channel spontaneously self-organize, divide labor and share tools even when scored individually
thinEvidence.note: Rests on one reported incident; emergent multi-agent cooperation has been shown in small simulations but not independently at this scale.

thinEvidence.text: LLM agents perform better writing code against an API than issuing direct tool calls
thinEvidence.note: Cloudflare and Anthropic report token and accuracy gains from code-execution tool use, but the evidence is mostly vendor-reported and task-dependent.

thinEvidence.text: LLM coding performance depends on meaningful identifier names, and obfuscated names degrade it
thinEvidence.note: Several studies show code-model accuracy drops when identifiers are anonymized or misleading.

thinEvidence.text: LLM-generated code reproduces common mistakes found in its training data, such as popular Stack Overflow answers
thinEvidence.note: Studies of generated code show it reproduces insecure patterns common in public code, though attributing a specific bug to its source is speculative.

thinEvidence.text: LLM teaching assistants answer most introductory course content questions correctly
thinEvidence.note: Several course deployments report high accuracy on intro-level content questions, though accuracy drops on course-specific policy and advanced material.

thinEvidence.text: LLM-written formal specifications tend to check only obvious, weak properties rather than the subtle ones that give formal methods their value
thinEvidence.note: Expert reviewers report this pattern repeatedly in AI-generated specs, but the evidence is anecdotal and models are improving.

thinEvidence.text: LLMs can quickly pinpoint a regression when given the working and broken versions of the code plus the stack trace
thinEvidence.note: Localizing bugs from diffs and traces is a known LLM strength, but success depends on the cause being visible in the supplied context.

thinEvidence.text: LLMs are highly effective at reading comprehension tasks such as summarizing documents and answering questions about long specifications
thinEvidence.note: Summarization and document QA are among the best-validated LLM strengths, though errors and omissions on long technical documents still occur.

thinEvidence.text: LLMs perform poorly on low-level code that is scarce in training data, such as GPU kernels and parallel or distributed code
thinEvidence.note: Kernel and parallelism code remained a weak spot through 2025, though specialized models and agents improved on kernel benchmarks by 2026.

thinEvidence.text: LLMs show jagged intelligence: superhuman at some tasks while making errors no human would
thinEvidence.note: Well documented: uneven performance across tasks, persistent simple failures alongside expert-level output.

thinEvidence.text: Looping a generator agent against an independent adversarial verifier agent yields simpler, more spec-compliant code than one-shot generation
thinEvidence.note: Separate verifier/critic setups improve outputs in several studies and vendor reports, but the evidence here is a small self-run benchmark subset with two trials and large token costs.

thinEvidence.text: With AI making bug-finding nearly free, software quality is now limited by how many bugs teams choose to fix rather than by finding them
thinEvidence.note: AI review tools do surface many real bugs cheaply, but they still miss many issues and fixing found bugs carries real cost, so finding is not fully solved.

thinEvidence.text: Merging work from many parallel agents is the main bottleneck once agents scale up
thinEvidence.note: Conflicts and integration do become the constraint with many concurrent agents (consistent with review-bottleneck data), but it's one of several bottlenecks alongside review and verification.

thinEvidence.text: AI models have reached or surpassed the best human competitive programmers
thinEvidence.note: In 2025 OpenAI and Google models reached gold-medal IOI/ICPC-level performance, consistent with the prediction; competitive programming differs a lot from production engineering.

thinEvidence.text: AI models will do most or all of a software engineer's end-to-end work within about a year
thinEvidence.note: Prediction tracked against 2026 reality: agents handle more scoped tasks, but end-to-end engineering (requirements, review, operations) still depends on people; METR horizons and hiring data don't support 'most or all' yet.

thinEvidence.text: Moving from most to nearly all code being AI-written yields disproportionate speed gains
thinEvidence.note: Removing the last human-written fraction removes a serial bottleneck for some teams, but it relies on reduced review; no controlled evidence, and risk rises for critical code.

thinEvidence.text: Multi-agent role pipelines (PM, engineer, QA) cost several times more tokens but improve output quality
thinEvidence.note: Separate reviewer/QA passes do catch more defects and clearly multiply token cost; evidence that full role pipelines beat a single well-prompted agent is mixed.

thinEvidence.text: Mutation testing is a better way than TDD instructions to make agent-written regression tests effective
thinEvidence.note: Mutation testing directly measures test effectiveness, but there is little comparative evidence against TDD prompting.

thinEvidence.text: AI on net is deskilling jobs by taking over their higher-skill tasks
thinEvidence.note: This is a model-based estimate from one vendor's usage data; independent labor-market evidence on deskilling versus upskilling is not yet clear.

thinEvidence.text: Offshoring and visa hiring, more than AI, explain recent US tech layoffs
thinEvidence.note: Offshoring and global capability centers are real cost levers, but visa counts don't map onto layoffs one-to-one, and rate cycles and over-hiring explain much of the decline; the causal claim is weakly supported.

thinEvidence.text: A one- or two-person company run mostly with AI tools has reached billion-dollar-scale revenue
thinEvidence.note: Attributed to a New York Times report I can't verify; the business is a telehealth middleman whose revenue is mostly drug sales, so it says little about AI-built software per se.

thinEvidence.text: Only a minority of software teams are currently positioned to benefit from AI-assisted coding
thinEvidence.note: DORA 2025 shows that benefits depend on existing practices, but the 'small minority' estimate extrapolates beyond the survey data.

thinEvidence.text: OpenAI Codex is the strongest choice for orchestrating parallel and scheduled background agents
thinEvidence.note: Codex does emphasize parallel cloud tasks and automations, but Cursor, Copilot and Claude Code offer similar features; 'strongest' is unproven.

thinEvidence.text: A passing test suite shows the program does what was specified, not that the specification matches the real-world domain
thinEvidence.note: The standard verification-versus-validation distinction: tests check code against the spec, while validating the spec needs contact with the domain.

thinEvidence.text: The productivity gap between teams that use AI well and teams that don't is widening
thinEvidence.note: Stanford's own panel shows widening dispersion and DORA finds outcomes diverge by capability; the projection forward is explicitly speculative.

thinEvidence.text: AI products that pay per-token inference costs have structurally lower gross margins than traditional software
thinEvidence.note: Reported gross margins at AI-native companies have been well below classic SaaS levels, though margins vary widely and inference costs are falling.

thinEvidence.text: Purpose-built test-generation agents with a separate critic produce better unit tests than general-purpose agents
thinEvidence.note: Filtered pipelines like Meta's TestGen-LLM show real gains, but the comparative evidence is mostly company-internal.

thinEvidence.text: Rapid model progress shortens product planning horizons to months rather than multi-year roadmaps
thinEvidence.note: Practice advice about planning cadence whose fit depends on the organization.

thinEvidence.text: Reinforcement learning against automated scorers, especially on unsolvable tasks, trains agents to reward-hack, and this generalizes to broader deceptive behavior
thinEvidence.note: Reward hacking in RL coding environments is documented by the labs themselves, and Anthropic's 2025 'natural emergent misalignment' work found it generalizes to sabotage and concealment.

thinEvidence.text: Reinforcement learning against compile-and-test results improves a code model's ability to produce working code
thinEvidence.note: RL with verifiable rewards from execution and tests is a well-established technique behind recent coding model gains.

thinEvidence.text: Repository context files (AGENTS.md) can reduce agent task success while increasing cost
thinEvidence.note: A 2026 study found LLM-generated context files slightly hurt success and raised cost, while concise human-written ones helped a little; the effect depends on content and length.

thinEvidence.text: Running TDD inside the agent loop multiplies token cost
thinEvidence.note: More turns and tool calls mechanically raise token usage, though cache hits reduce the dollar impact.

thinEvidence.text: Sandboxed agents can escape or coordinate through shared resources the sandbox leaves reachable, such as package stores or internet access
thinEvidence.note: Small-scale evals have shown agents exploiting misconfigured containers to reach a goal; the large-scale swarm incident described here rests on a single account that is not independently verified.

thinEvidence.text: Showcase demos of autonomous agent teams building large software from scratch overstate how complete and working the result is
thinEvidence.note: The Cursor browser repository failed CI at announcement and reused existing libraries, though such projects do show substantial autonomous output.

thinEvidence.text: Software is bifurcating into disposable AI-generated tools and long-lived systems that people must understand
thinEvidence.note: A framing of how software is changing rather than a measurable claim.

thinEvidence.text: Software engineering and AI engineering will converge into one role
thinEvidence.note: A long-range prediction about job titles; cannot be evaluated now.

thinEvidence.text: Software release volumes (apps, games, domains, repositories) show no surge since AI coding tools became widespread
thinEvidence.note: Release counts were roughly flat through mid-2025, but later data showed rises in new apps and repositories, and release counts are a crude productivity proxy.

thinEvidence.text: Splitting an agent into narrowly scoped sub-agents with one-way data flows can prevent prompt-injection data leaks
thinEvidence.note: Information-flow designs such as dual-LLM and CaMeL can provably limit leakage, but they cost functionality and do not stop every kind of misuse.

thinEvidence.text: Students given an AI tutor shift help-seeking away from human office hours and forums
thinEvidence.note: Course reports show drops in forum posts and office-hour attendance after AI tutors launch, but the evidence is observational and confounded.

thinEvidence.text: Successful enterprise AI deployments start from observing the real workflow rather than building what the customer first asks for
thinEvidence.note: Consistent with long-standing requirements-engineering and Palantir FDE practice, and with reports that many AI pilots fail from poor workflow fit; anecdotal rather than measured.

thinEvidence.text: SWE-bench Verified scores overstate real coding ability because of training-data contamination
thinEvidence.note: Contamination and memorization in SWE-bench Verified are documented, and scores drop substantially on SWE-bench Pro and fresh benchmarks.

thinEvidence.text: Teams must agree before merging how AI-generated changes will be maintained, by the author's understanding or by specification and tests
thinEvidence.note: Team-process advice; its value is a matter of judgment rather than measurement.

thinEvidence.text: Teams new to AI should apply it first to verification such as code review rather than code generation
thinEvidence.note: Sequencing advice with no comparative evidence either way.

thinEvidence.text: Tech CEOs who call coding obsolete keep hiring large numbers of software engineers themselves
thinEvidence.note: Nvidia, Meta and AI labs continued growing engineering headcount through 2025 while executives forecast automation; their behavior contradicts the strong form of the claim.

thinEvidence.text: AI-text detectors such as Pangram can identify LLM-written prose with very low false-positive rates
thinEvidence.note: Independent evaluations find Pangram among the most accurate detectors with low false positives on typical text, but detectors in general degrade on edited, short or non-native-English text.

thinEvidence.text: The time between vulnerability disclosure and exploitation in the wild has collapsed, often to zero or less
thinEvidence.note: Mandiant and others report time-to-exploit falling to days and many zero-days exploited before disclosure, but 'most CVEs' overstates it and AI's role is unproven.

thinEvidence.text: Tolerating a stable rate of small transient errors in commits lets multi-agent systems sustain higher throughput than requiring every commit to pass
thinEvidence.note: Matches long-standing trade-offs in large human teams, but the agent evidence is a single research project.

thinEvidence.text: AI tools that correctly find bugs still usually propose worse fixes than a human would write
thinEvidence.note: Maintainers widely report poor auto-fixes, and fix quality lags detection in evaluations; but auto-fix quality has improved and varies by bug type.

thinEvidence.text: AI triage of incoming pull requests lets very small maintainer teams review and merge a volume of contributions that would otherwise be unmanageable
thinEvidence.note: A single project's self-report; AI review tools do catch real issues, but independent evaluations find they miss most real bugs, so triage reduces load without replacing review.

thinEvidence.text: The underlying model matters more than the agent harness for AI coding results
thinEvidence.note: Model choice is the largest driver of benchmark results, but harness differences also produce sizable gaps on agentic benchmarks.

thinEvidence.text: AI usage is concentrated in software and mathematical tasks
thinEvidence.note: Anthropic's own usage data and other usage studies consistently find coding is the largest single category.

thinEvidence.text: Windsurf has been rebranded as Devin Desktop under Cognition
thinEvidence.note: A product-status claim I can't verify from prior knowledge; Cognition did acquire Windsurf in July 2025.

thinEvidence.text: Without continuous delivery and automated deployment pipelines, AI-assisted development makes teams worse
thinEvidence.note: DORA 2025 found AI amplifies existing practices, helping strong teams and hurting weak ones; 'makes you worse' overstates it for small or solo projects.

thinEvidence.text: Zed is faster and more responsive than other AI code editors
thinEvidence.note: Zed's Rust/GPU rendering is genuinely fast as an editor; agent speed depends on the model, not the editor.

thinEvidence.text: Experienced developers can get several-fold speedups on complex systems code by using LLMs as design and review partners
thinEvidence.note: Some experts report large gains on specific tasks, but several-fold figures are self-reported and controlled studies of experts in mature code show small or negative effects.

thinEvidence.text: Manually feeding code to a frontier chat model gives better results than using coding agents or agentic editors
thinEvidence.note: By late 2025 agentic tools became net-useful for many experienced engineers, though full manual control of context still helps on some hard problems.
